9|9,10|Course susceptibility table|Using the supplied course table, a tetracycline zone is 16 mm. Which category applies?|Moderately sensitive|Sensitive|Resistant|Cannot be measured in millimeters|The course table places tetracycline zones of 15-18 mm in the moderately sensitive category; this exercise uses that classroom table.

9|9,10|Course susceptibility table|Using the supplied course table, what does a 20 mm tetracycline zone indicate?|Sensitive|Moderately sensitive|Resistant|No inhibition|The supplied table defines tetracycline sensitivity at 19 mm or more; the question is an interpretation of this course table.

7|1|Fungal structure|Which cellular feature distinguishes the eukaryotic microbes studied in this lab from bacteria?|A membrane-enclosed nucleus|A peptidoglycan cell wall|A nucleoid without a nuclear membrane|A capsule made of bacterial slime|Eukaryotes compartmentalize their DNA in a nucleus and contain membrane-enclosed organelles.

7|1|Fungal nutrition|How do fungi obtain carbon and energy?|By absorbing organic nutrients|By fixing carbon through chlorophyll|By oxidizing only inorganic minerals|By ingesting food with an oral groove|Fungi are heterotrophic and nonphotosynthetic; they absorb organic material from their surroundings.

7|1|Fungal structure|Which polymer is a characteristic component of fungal cell walls?|Chitin|Peptidoglycan|Lipopolysaccharide|Glycogen alone|Chitin is a structural wall polymer; peptidoglycan is a bacterial wall component.

7|1|Fungal reproduction|Which process most commonly produces a new Saccharomyces cell?|Budding|Endospore formation|Formation of a scolex|Production of a protozoan cyst|Yeasts commonly reproduce asexually by budding from the parent cell.

7|1|Fungal classification|In the classification used by this course, which feature is central to grouping fungi?|The type of sexual spore produced|The number of bacterial flagella|The presence of a Gram-negative outer membrane|The number of nuclei in a bacterial nucleoid|The module groups fungi by sexual spores such as ascospores, basidiospores and zygospores.

7|1|Mold observation|Which observations help distinguish mold colonies macroscopically?|Texture, pigmentation and mycelial growth|Only the pH of the stain|Only the number of bacterial endospores|Only the presence of red blood cells|The worksheet asks for colony texture, center and edge pigmentation, and growth above and into the agar.

7|2|Mold microscopy|Which stain is used for the tape preparation of mold in this lab?|Lactophenol cotton blue|Neutral red in MacConkey agar|Oxidase reagent|Nitrate reagents A and B|The mold tape preparation is placed over lactophenol cotton blue to visualize fungal structures.

7|2|Mold microscopy|Which reproductive structure should be sought in a Rhizopus preparation?|Sporangia containing spores|A bacterial capsule surrounding cocci|An oral groove with cilia|A tapeworm scolex|The module identifies Rhizopus sporangiophores, sporangia and spores, as well as sexual structures.

7|2|Mold microscopy|Which structures should be identified in Aspergillus and Penicillium preparations?|Conidiophores with chains of conidia|Proglottids containing reproductive organs|Flagella with an undulating membrane|Endospores inside bacterial rods|The worksheet specifically calls for hyphae, conidiophores and chains of conidia in these molds.

7|2|Yeast microscopy|Which dye is used to observe Saccharomyces cerevisiae in this lab?|Methylene blue|Phenol red|Bromothymol blue|Nitrate reagent A|The yeast wet mount uses methylene blue; the other chemicals serve different biochemical tests.

7|2|Yeast identification|After morphology suggests a yeast genus, what is commonly needed to distinguish species?|Biochemical tests|Measurement of a scolex|Counting only fungal hyphae|Observation of bacterial pili alone|The source distinguishes genus-level morphology from biochemical testing used to differentiate yeast species.

7|3|Protozoa|A protozoan is actively feeding and moving. Which life-cycle stage is being observed?|Trophozoite|Cyst|Proglottid|Basidiospore|The trophozoite is the active feeding stage; the cyst is a resistant dormant form.

7|3|Protozoa|Which feature makes a protozoan cyst important in transmission?|Resistance during unfavorable conditions|Rapid budding into yeast cells|Production of a fungal mycelium|Continuous photosynthesis in every species|A cyst is a resistant dormant structure that can help protozoa survive outside a favorable host environment.

7|3|Protist metabolism|Why can Euglena grow differently in light and darkness?|It can photosynthesize in light and use organic nutrients without light|It changes from a bacterium into a fungus|It loses all ability to obtain energy in darkness|It always requires a vertebrate host|The course describes Euglena as a photosynthetic flagellate capable of chemoheterotrophic metabolism without light.

7|3|Protist microscopy|An unstained protist wet mount has very little contrast. Which adjustment can improve visibility?|Reduce illumination by adjusting the condenser or iris|Add nitrate reagents to the specimen|Use oil immersion for every specimen|Open the iris fully and maximize light|The worksheet recommends limiting light because unstained wet mounts have little contrast.

7|3|Protozoan motility|Which structure is used by Amoeba and Entamoeba for movement and ingestion?|Pseudopodia|Conidiophores|Proglottids|Sporangia|Amoebae extend cytoplasmic pseudopodia for locomotion and engulfment.
7|3|Ciliates|Which protist group includes Paramecium and Balantidium?|Ciliates|Cestodes|Zygomycetes|Nematodes|The listed ciliates use cilia for motility and nutrient gathering.

7|3|Dinoflagellates|Why can a red-tide bloom make shellfish unsafe to eat?|Dinoflagellate toxins can accumulate in marine food|The shellfish become bacterial endospores|All marine algae develop a scolex|Salt is completely removed from the water|The module connects dinoflagellate blooms with neurotoxins and illness after consuming contaminated seafood.

7|4|Apicomplexans|Where should the ring-stage trophozoite of Plasmodium be sought?|Inside red blood cells|Inside fungal sporangia|On a tapeworm scolex|Within a bacterial endospore|The worksheet specifically identifies Plasmodium ring-stage trophozoites in erythrocytes.

7|4|Algal morphology|Which feature should be identified in a Volvox preparation?|A colony containing daughter colonies|A segmented body with a scolex|A chain of fungal conidia|A Gram-negative outer membrane|Volvox is examined for its colonial arrangement and daughter colonies.

7|4|Helminths|Which structure attaches a tapeworm to its host?|Scolex|Mycelium|Contractile vacuole|Conidiophore|The tapeworm head, or scolex, bears attachment structures; proglottids are its body segments.

7|4|Helminths|A worm is cylindrical with separate male and female individuals. Which group fits best?|Nematodes|Cestodes|Trematodes|Ciliates|The module describes nematodes as cylindrical roundworms that are dioecious.

7|4|Helminths|Which description best fits a trematode adult?|A leaf-shaped fluke with suckers|A budding unicellular yeast|A filamentous alga with spiral chloroplasts|A segmented tapeworm composed of proglottids|Trematodes are flukes; their leaf-shaped bodies and suckers distinguish them from tapeworms and roundworms.

8|1|Viable counts|Why are plate-count results expressed as CFU rather than an exact number of individual cells?|One colony may arise from one cell or a cluster of cells|Every visible colony contains exactly one cell|Dead cells always form colonies|CFU measures only the amount of agar|A colony-forming unit is a viable unit capable of generating a colony, which may include attached cells.
8|1|Serial dilution|What dilution results from adding 1 mL of culture to 9 mL of diluent?|10^-1|10^-2|10^-9|10^1|The culture is one part of a total volume of ten parts, giving a one-in-ten dilution.
8|1,3|Serial dilution|Four consecutive 1:10 dilutions give which final dilution?|10^-4|10^-1|10^-8|4 x 10^-1|Successive dilution fractions multiply: one tenth raised to the fourth power equals 10^-4.

8|3|Serial dilution|What dilution results from adding 1 mL of culture to 99 mL of diluent?|10^-2|10^-1|10^-3|10^-99|The sample occupies 1 mL of a 100 mL total volume, giving a one-in-one-hundred dilution.

8|1,3|Countable plates|Which plate falls within the countable range specified in this lab?|A plate with 125 colonies|A plate with 12 colonies|A plate with 450 colonies|A plate with confluent growth|The protocol uses plates with 30 to 300 colonies; very small counts and overcrowded plates are unreliable.

8|1|CFU calculations|A 1 mL inoculum from a 10^-3 dilution produces 50 colonies. What is the original concentration?|5.0 x 10^4 CFU/mL|5.0 x 10^3 CFU/mL|5.0 x 10^5 CFU/mL|5.0 x 10^2 CFU/mL|Divide 50 by the dilution fraction 10^-3 and the plated volume of 1 mL.

8|1|CFU calculations|A 0.1 mL inoculum from a 10^-3 dilution produces 50 colonies. What is the original concentration?|5.0 x 10^5 CFU/mL|5.0 x 10^4 CFU/mL|5.0 x 10^3 CFU/mL|5.0 x 10^6 CFU/mL|CFU/mL equals colonies divided by dilution times volume: 50 divided by 10^-3 times 0.1.

8|1,3|CFU calculations|Duplicate plates inoculated with 0.1 mL of a 10^-6 dilution contain 80 and 100 colonies. What concentration follows from their mean?|9.0 x 10^8 CFU/mL|9.0 x 10^7 CFU/mL|1.8 x 10^9 CFU/mL|9.0 x 10^6 CFU/mL|The mean is 90 colonies; dividing by 10^-6 times 0.1 mL gives 9.0 x 10^8 CFU/mL.

8|2|Dilution technique|Why must each dilution tube be mixed before transferring the next aliquot?|To distribute cells throughout the sample|To sterilize the cells|To reverse the dilution|To convert dead cells into viable cells|Uneven cell distribution produces an unrepresentative aliquot and distorts later dilution counts.

8|2|Dilution technique|Why is a fresh sterile tip used for each dilution transfer?|To prevent carryover and contamination|To increase bacterial growth during transfer|To remove the need for mixing|To make every dilution 1:100|Fresh tips help preserve the intended dilution and prevent cross-contamination.

8|2|Spread plating|Why should a sterilized glass spreader cool before touching the inoculum?|A hot spreader could kill viable cells|Cooling removes the need for incubation|Cooling makes the dilution ten times stronger|A cold spreader creates colonies without cells|The count depends on viable cells surviving spreading; residual heat can reduce recovery.

8|1,3|Viable counts|Why can a standard plate count underestimate all cells actually present?|Only cells able to grow under the culture conditions form colonies|It counts every dead cell twice|It counts only fungal hyphae|It measures all cells without requiring growth|Viable plate counts depend on the medium, atmosphere and incubation conditions permitting colony formation.

8|1|Volume correction|What happens to the calculated CFU/mL if a 0.1 mL plated volume is mistakenly treated as 1 mL?|The estimate is tenfold too low|The estimate is tenfold too high|The estimate stays correct|The estimate becomes zero|The missing volume correction omits a factor of ten from the original-sample concentration.

8|3|Replicates|Why are replicate plates useful in a standard plate count?|They reduce the influence of sampling variation|They guarantee every cell is a different species|They eliminate dilution calculations|They allow confluent plates to be counted accurately|Small sampling differences are expected; replicate counts improve the estimate when averaged appropriately.

9|1|Culture media|Which property defines a chemically defined medium?|The identity and quantity of every ingredient are known|It contains an unidentified tissue extract|It always contains blood|It can grow every microorganism|Complex media include ingredients of incompletely known composition, whereas defined media have specified chemical components.

9|1|Growth requirements|A bacterium grows in BHI broth but not in nutrient or glucose-salts broth. What does this suggest?|It is relatively fastidious|It cannot grow in any medium|It must be photosynthetic|It can synthesize every required nutrient|Growth only in the richer medium suggests additional nutritional requirements.

9|2|MSA selectivity|Which MSA ingredient provides its high-salt selection?|7.5% sodium chloride|Mannitol|Phenol red|Neutral red|The salt selects salt-tolerant organisms; mannitol and phenol red provide the fermentation differential.

9|2|MSA interpretation|An organism grows on MSA and turns the surrounding agar yellow. What does this indicate?|Salt tolerance and acid production from mannitol|Salt intolerance and no fermentation|Lactose fermentation without growth|Nitrate reduction to nitrogen gas|Growth demonstrates tolerance of the medium; yellow phenol red indicates acidification associated with mannitol fermentation.

9|2,3|MSA interpretation|An organism does not grow on MSA. What can be concluded about mannitol fermentation?|Its mannitol-fermentation ability cannot be determined from this plate|It definitely cannot ferment mannitol|It definitely ferments mannitol|It must ferment lactose instead|The selective conditions prevented growth, so the differential reaction cannot be interpreted.

9|3|Osmotic pressure|How do high salt or sugar concentrations inhibit many microbes in preserved foods?|They draw water out of cells by osmosis|They supply extra water to cells|They directly remove all DNA|They make the environment isotonic for every organism|A hypertonic environment favors water loss and can cause plasmolysis and inhibited growth.

9|3|Oxygen gradients|What is the role of sodium thioglycollate in FTB?|It consumes oxygen and helps establish an oxygen gradient|It supplies nitrate reagents|It stains all growing cells purple|It ferments mannitol|Thioglycollate reduces oxygen while oxygen diffuses in from the top, allowing different growth positions.

9|3|Oxygen indicators|What does a pink region in fluid thioglycollate broth indicate?|Oxidized resazurin where oxygen is present|An anaerobic zone with no oxygen|A positive lactose test|Nitrate reduction after zinc|Resazurin is pink when oxidized and colorless when reduced.

9|3,4|Aerotolerance|Growth occurs only at the top of an oxygen-gradient tube. Which category fits best?|Obligate aerobe|Obligate anaerobe|Aerotolerant anaerobe|Facultative anaerobe|An obligate aerobe requires oxygen and grows where its concentration is greatest.

9|3,4|Aerotolerance|Growth occurs only near the bottom of an oxygen-gradient tube. Which category fits best?|Obligate anaerobe|Obligate aerobe|Microaerophile|Facultative anaerobe|An obligate anaerobe grows in the region with the least oxygen and is inhibited by oxygen exposure.

9|3,4|Aerotolerance|Growth occurs throughout FTB but is heaviest at the top. Which category fits best?|Facultative anaerobe|Obligate aerobe|Obligate anaerobe|Aerotolerant anaerobe|Facultative anaerobes can grow without oxygen but usually grow better when oxygen is available.

9|3,4|Aerotolerance|Growth is fairly even throughout FTB. Which oxygen relationship is most consistent with this pattern?|Aerotolerant anaerobe|Obligate aerobe|Obligate anaerobe|Microaerophile|Aerotolerant anaerobes tolerate oxygen but do not gain the same growth advantage from it as facultative anaerobes.

9|3,4|Aerotolerance|A narrow band of growth occurs just below the surface of FTB. Which category fits best?|Microaerophile|Obligate aerobe|Obligate anaerobe|Aerotolerant anaerobe|Microaerophiles require oxygen at concentrations below those in air.

9|4|Oxygen gradients|Why should an incubated FTB tube remain unshaken before it is read?|Shaking can redistribute oxygen and obscure the growth pattern|Shaking turns every colony Gram-positive|Shaking destroys the pH indicator permanently|Shaking converts nitrate into nitrite|The location of growth relative to the oxygen gradient is the evidence used to classify aerotolerance.

9|5,6|Temperature|Why can high temperatures be lethal while refrigeration often only slows growth?|High heat can denature enzymes, whereas cold often slows metabolism|Cold always destroys all bacterial DNA|Heat always stimulates enzyme activity indefinitely|Refrigeration converts bacteria into viruses|The module distinguishes reduced enzymatic activity below the minimum from damage above the maximum temperature.

9|5|Temperature|Which three temperatures describe an organism's cardinal temperatures?|Minimum, optimum and maximum|Freezing, boiling and room temperature|Morning, noon and evening|Growth, death and dilution|Cardinal temperatures define the lower limit, best growth temperature and upper limit of growth.

9|5,6|Temperature|Which group best fits microbes adapted to high-temperature hot springs?|Thermophiles|Mesophiles|Neutrophiles|Halotolerant bacteria|Thermophiles are classified by high-temperature growth; neutrophily concerns pH and halotolerance concerns salt.

9|6|UV damage|What DNA lesion is a major result of ultraviolet exposure?|Pyrimidine dimers|A new fungal nucleus|A bacterial capsule|An extra peptidoglycan layer|Adjacent pyrimidines can become linked, interfering with normal replication and transcription.

9|6,7|UV controls|Why is a zero-second UV plate included?|It provides an unexposed growth control|It measures nitrate reduction|It guarantees every exposed cell is dead|It supplies extra UV energy|The unexposed plate establishes growth without UV treatment for comparison with exposed plates.

9|7|UV repair|Why are plates covered with foil after UV exposure?|To reduce light-dependent DNA repair|To increase oxygen penetration|To promote photosynthesis|To supply nutrients|Foil blocks light that could activate photoreactivation and reduce the measured UV effect.

9|6,7|UV penetration|Why can leaving a plastic lid on a plate reduce the UV effect?|Ordinary plastic limits UV penetration to the cells|The lid generates new bacteria|The lid turns UV into an antibiotic|UV passes through plastic more effectively than air|The module emphasizes the limited penetration of UV through ordinary glass and plastic.
9|7,8|pH|How much greater is hydrogen ion concentration at pH 3 than at pH 7?|10,000 times|4 times|40 times|100 times|Each pH unit represents a tenfold change; four units correspond to 10^4.

9|8|pH data|An organism grows most abundantly at pH 3 and not at pH 9 or 11. Which classification fits?|Acidophile|Alkaliphile|Neutrophile|Thermophile|The preferred acidic conditions identify an acidophile; thermal classification requires temperature data.

9|8|Disk diffusion|What does a clear area around an antimicrobial disk show directly?|Growth was inhibited under the assay conditions|The organism is automatically clinically susceptible|Every cell on the plate was killed|The antibiotic must have the lowest MIC|A zone shows inhibition; standardized interpretation is needed before classifying antibiotic susceptibility.

9|8,9|Kirby-Bauer|How should an antibiotic inhibition zone be interpreted?|Measure its diameter in millimeters and compare with the appropriate standard|Measure only its radius and compare all drugs with one cutoff|Call any visible zone susceptible|Ignore the organism and antibiotic identity|Susceptibility interpretation depends on the relevant organism-drug standard, not on zone presence alone.

9|8,9|Disk diffusion|Why can two disinfectants form different zone sizes even if both inhibit growth?|Their diffusion through agar may differ|Larger zones always prove greater clinical efficacy|Every chemical has the same diffusion rate|Zone size depends only on colony pigment|Molecular properties affect diffusion, so zone sizes across agents require careful comparison.

9|9|Kirby-Bauer medium|Which agar is used for antimicrobial disk diffusion in the module?|Mueller-Hinton agar|Mannitol salt agar|MacConkey agar|PEA agar|The protocol uses Mueller-Hinton plates for the standardized bacterial lawn assay.

9|11|Selective toxicity|Why is selective toxicity desirable in an antimicrobial drug?|It harms the microbe more than the host|It damages host and microbial cells equally|It makes all drugs broad-spectrum|It prevents all future mutations|Drugs ideally exploit differences between the pathogen and host cells.

9|11|Antimicrobial resistance|Why can inappropriate antibiotic use select for resistance?|Resistant variants survive and reproduce while susceptible cells are suppressed|The host's cells become bacterial spores|Every bacterium intentionally mutates to the same drug|Antibiotics permanently prevent gene transfer|Natural selection increases the proportion of resistant organisms under drug exposure.

10|1|Biochemical identification|Why can Gram staining alone fail to identify a bacterial species?|Different species can share the same Gram reaction and morphology|Every bacterium has the same genome|Gram staining measures all metabolic pathways|Only viruses can be Gram stained|The source lists Gram-negative rods that look similar after staining but differ in biochemical reactions.

10|1|pH indicators|What does phenol red becoming yellow indicate in these fermentation media?|Acid production|An alkaline reaction|No change in pH|A positive oxidase reaction|Phenol red is yellow below about pH 6.8; acid from carbohydrate metabolism can produce this change.

10|1|PEA agar|Which organisms does PEA primarily select for?|Gram-positive bacteria|Gram-negative enteric bacteria|Only acid-fast bacteria|Only viruses|PEA inhibits many Gram-negative organisms and is used to recover Gram-positive bacteria from mixtures.

10|1|PEA agar|Why should growth on PEA be compared with growth on TSA?|The comparison helps distinguish selective inhibition from general failure to grow|TSA is a lactose indicator|Both media selectively inhibit Gram-positive cells|TSA determines oxidase activity|A general-purpose control shows whether the organism can grow under the incubation conditions.

10|1,2|MacConkey selectivity|Which MacConkey ingredients inhibit many Gram-positive organisms?|Bile salts and crystal violet|Mannitol and sodium chloride|Phenol red and glucose|Nitrate reagents A and B|The selective ingredients are bile salts and crystal violet; lactose and neutral red provide the differential system.

10|1,2|MacConkey differentiation|Pink colonies on MacConkey agar most directly indicate what?|Acid production from lactose fermentation|Mannitol fermentation on high-salt medium|Positive catalase activity|Complete blood-cell lysis|Lactose fermentation acidifies the medium and changes the neutral-red indicator.

10|1,2|MacConkey differentiation|A Gram-negative isolate grows as colorless colonies on MacConkey agar. What is the best interpretation?|Growth without detectable lactose fermentation|Failure to tolerate the selective medium|Positive oxidase activity|Proof of a pure Salmonella culture|Colorless growth supports a non-lactose-fermenting result, but does not identify a species on its own.

10|2|Mixed cultures|Why are mixed cultures streaked onto selective media?|To separate organisms and obtain isolated colonies|To make every colony the same species|To replace all later biochemical tests|To convert Gram-negative cells into Gram-positive cells|Streaking separates cells while selective media favor different components of the mixture.

10|3|Microbiota interpretation|No growth occurs from a body-site swab on either selective plate. What can be concluded?|The organisms may be inhibited or unable to grow under these conditions|The sampled site is definitely sterile|The sample contains only viruses|All bacteria at that site are lactose fermenters|A negative culture on selective media does not establish absence of microorganisms at the site.

10|4|Culture purity|After subculturing an isolated colony, what helps assess purity?|Colony morphology together with Gram staining|The sample label alone|The pH of the disinfectant alone|An oxidase reagent left in air for several minutes|Consistent colonies and microscopic morphology support purity; a label does not demonstrate it.

10|4,5|Blood agar|Which result represents beta hemolysis on blood agar?|A transparent zone of complete red-cell lysis|A green-brown zone of partial breakdown|Growth with no visible change in the agar|A pink colony caused by lactose fermentation|Beta hemolysis is complete lysis; alpha is partial breakdown and gamma describes no visible hemolysis.

10|4,5|Blood agar|Which result represents alpha hemolysis?|Green-brown discoloration around growth|A transparent zone of complete lysis|No change around colonies|A yellow Durham tube|Alpha hemolysis produces partial hemoglobin breakdown and green-brown discoloration.

10|5|PR broth|A PR-glucose broth is yellow and contains a bubble in its Durham tube. How should it be recorded?|Acid positive and gas positive|Acid negative and gas positive|Acid positive and gas negative|Peptonization positive with no fermentation|Yellow broth indicates acid, and the trapped bubble indicates gas production.

10|5|PR broth|What does a Durham tube detect in a fermentation broth?|Gas production|The number of chromosomes|The Gram reaction|The presence of a capsule|The inverted small tube traps gas released during metabolism.

10|5|PR broth|What most directly explains bright pink PR broth?|Alkaline products from peptonization|Acid from carbohydrate fermentation|Nitrite reacting with zinc|A positive blood-agar hemolysis reaction|Protein and amino-acid metabolism can release ammonia and raise the pH.

10|5,8|PR broth|A PR broth is yellow at 24 hours but bright pink later. What is a possible explanation?|Sugar was depleted and peptone metabolism produced alkaline compounds|The organism changed its Gram reaction|Nitrite was converted directly to lactose|The Durham tube removed every acid molecule|Peptonization after sugar depletion can reverse an initially acidic reaction; timing matters when interpreting cultures.

10|6|Nitrate reduction|What reaction is catalyzed by nitrate reductase in this assay?|Nitrate is reduced to nitrite|Nitrite is oxidized into lactose|Glucose is reduced to mannitol|Hydrogen peroxide is converted into nitrate|The assay asks whether organisms can use nitrate and reduce it to nitrite or further products.

10|6|Nitrate reduction|A nitrate broth turns red after reagents A and B, before zinc. What is the result?|Positive for nitrate reduction to nitrite|Negative for nitrate reduction|Positive only for catalase|Inconclusive until zinc is added|Reagents A and B detect nitrite; a red reaction at this step is positive.

10|6|Nitrate reduction|Why is a colorless nitrate broth after reagents A and B inconclusive?|Nitrate may be unchanged or reduced beyond nitrite|Colorless always means no bacteria grew|Nitrite always makes the broth blue|Zinc is needed to detect lactose|Both unreduced nitrate and further reduction beyond nitrite can produce no initial red reaction.

10|6|Nitrate reduction|A colorless broth turns red after zinc is added. How is this interpreted?|Negative: nitrate remained and zinc reduced it chemically|Positive: bacteria reduced nitrate beyond nitrite|Positive: catalase released oxygen|Negative: lactose was exhausted|Zinc converts remaining nitrate to nitrite; the red color therefore reveals nitrate not reduced by the organism.

10|6|Nitrate reduction|A broth remains colorless after reagents A and B and then zinc. What is the interpretation in this assay?|Positive for nitrate reduction beyond nitrite|Negative because the zinc must always turn red|Positive for mannitol fermentation only|Proof of an obligate aerobe|No detectable nitrate remains for zinc to reduce, consistent with reduction to later nitrogen products.

10|6|Nitrate gas|Why is gas in nitrate broth not conclusive evidence of denitrification for a fermenter?|Fermentation may also produce gas|Only oxidase-positive organisms make gas|Zinc is present before inoculation|Gas cannot enter a Durham tube|A known fermenter can generate gas by a pathway other than nitrate reduction.
10|7|Oxidase|Which enzyme is detected by the oxidase test?|Cytochrome c oxidase|Nitrate reductase|Catalase|Lactase|The reagent reports cytochrome c oxidase activity in electron transport.

10|7|Oxidase timing|A DrySlide turns purple only after two minutes. How should it be read using this course protocol?|Do not count the late color as a positive oxidase reaction|Record a positive reaction regardless of timing|Record a positive nitrate test|Record a positive catalase test|The protocol requires a purple reaction within 20 seconds; later color can reflect reagent autooxidation.

10|7|Oxidase interpretation|A DrySlide becomes dark purple within 20 seconds. What does that indicate?|A positive oxidase reaction|A negative oxidase reaction|Lactose fermentation|Nitrate remaining after zinc|Timely purple color is the positive endpoint specified for this oxidase assay.

10|7,8|Catalase|What causes bubbles in a positive catalase test?|Oxygen released from hydrogen peroxide|Carbon dioxide from lactose fermentation|Nitrogen released by zinc|Air produced by a Gram stain|Catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; the oxygen appears as bubbles.

10|8|Catalase controls|Why is a known catalase-positive control useful?|It checks that the hydrogen peroxide reagent is working|It makes all unknowns positive|It replaces the unknown culture|It establishes the organism's Gram reaction|A failed reagent could cause a false negative; the positive control verifies reagent activity.

10|8|Catalase sampling|Why should blood agar be avoided as the source of material for a catalase test?|Blood components can contribute catalase and confuse interpretation|Blood agar contains no nutrients|Blood agar always destroys hydrogen peroxide before sampling|All blood-agar colonies are obligate anaerobes|The module excludes blood agar because the test should reflect the isolate's enzyme rather than blood-derived activity.

10|8|Catalase differentiation|Which catalase result commonly distinguishes Staphylococcus from Streptococcus in the module?|Staphylococcus is positive; Streptococcus is negative|Both are always positive|Staphylococcus is negative; Streptococcus is positive|Both are always oxidase-positive|Catalase is commonly used to separate these Gram-positive cocci groups.

10|7,8|Oxygen defense|Which sequence correctly pairs the enzymes that detoxify superoxide and hydrogen peroxide?|Superoxide dismutase acts on superoxide; catalase acts on hydrogen peroxide|Catalase acts on nitrate; oxidase acts on lactose|Nitrate reductase acts on superoxide; catalase acts on mannitol|Both enzymes directly synthesize bacterial capsules|SOD helps convert superoxide to peroxide, and catalase removes peroxide by producing water and oxygen.
